title: Regeneration of a functioning growth plate

concept.text: The innovation would restore an injured, still-open growth plate—the cartilage structure that lengthens a child’s long bone—so that it resumes sustained, appropriately coordinated growth. Injury can create a bony bridge, or bar, across this tissue, interrupting growth and causing shortening or angular deformity. Successful regeneration would restore the growth function of the damaged region while preventing recurrent pathological bridging.

The target is living tissue with an organized growth process, rather than cartilage that merely fills a defect. The research identifies proliferative and hypertrophic cartilage organization as part of that intended architecture, but the supplied abstract does not substantiate those specific tissue-zone details. The essential functional distinction is supported: regenerated tissue must sustain longitudinal growth without forming a recurrent bone bridge. Normal cartilage turnover, replacement by bone during growth, and eventual skeletal maturation must remain possible; permanent preservation of all cartilage would be the wrong objective.

This entry concerns repair of an injured open physis. Reopening a mature, closed growth plate, increasing height in idiopathic short stature, treating idiopathic scoliosis, or reshaping the craniofacial skeleton would each require separate biological and clinical demonstrations. None follows automatically from successful repair of a childhood growth-plate injury.

significance.text: Restoring the tissue that generates bone length would address the cause of progressive deformity after physeal arrest. If the repaired region grew in coordination with the remaining plate, it could prevent additional limb-length discrepancy and angulation attributable to that arrest. The revolutionary capability would be recovery of the growth organ’s function, rather than a one-time change in bone geometry.

A plausible downstream benefit would be fewer later corrective procedures and less accumulated deformity during childhood. These are conditional clinical consequences, not outcomes demonstrated in the supplied evidence. Restoring future growth also does not necessarily reverse shortening or angulation that already exists; correction of established deformity would need to be measured separately.

As a conceptual comparison, limb lengthening and guided growth address length or alignment, whereas this innovation aims to restore damaged growth-generating tissue. The supplied evidence does not establish comparative effectiveness, recurrence rates, or reductions in osteotomies relative to those treatments. It also does not substantiate the earlier infection-specific benefit claim. Benefits after different causes of physeal injury would need separate evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is durable restoration of functional growth-plate cartilage after injury, with continued longitudinal growth and no recurrent pathological bone bridge. Rasouli and Wenke describe conventional bone-bridge resection and interpositional grafting as frequently failing to restore native physeal architecture or biological function, with common recurrence. Removing the obstruction therefore does not by itself establish regeneration of the tissue that should occupy the defect.

Engineering synthesis: a repair would need to establish an organized, self-maintaining cartilage growth process, integrate it with the surviving physis and adjacent bone, and coordinate growth across the plate. Producing cartilage in a defect would be insufficient if it did not generate length, grew unevenly, or subsequently became a pathological bridge. The desired control must distinguish normal cartilage-to-bone progression from premature bridging rather than suppressing all ossification.

Rasouli and Wenke discuss cell-based therapies, tissue-engineering scaffolds, gene therapies, growth-factor delivery, and exosome-based therapies as potential approaches. Their inclusion in a review identifies candidate strategies, not demonstrated solutions. A convincing breakthrough would have to show that a strategy restores sustained function, rather than only improving tissue appearance or temporarily reducing bridge formation.

Engineering synthesis: durability must extend through a changing developmental environment. A regenerated region would need to grow sufficiently and proportionately during remaining childhood growth, tolerate its anatomical setting, and eventually mature appropriately. Controlling that trajectory over years is a different requirement from showing short-term cartilage formation.

current_state.text: Rasouli and Wenke’s review in Annals of Biomedical Engineering, volume 54, pages 1126–1152, was electronically published on 19 December 2025, with DOI 10.1007/s10439-025-03942-5. Its abstract reports that growth-plate injuries account for up to 30% of pediatric fractures and describes the connection between bony bars, impaired longitudinal growth, limb-length discrepancy, angular deformity, and premature growth arrest. The percentage is an attributed review estimate; the supplied material does not independently validate its epidemiological basis. The retained evidence is the abstract record, not the full review.

That abstract supports the limitations of bridge resection and interpositional grafting and describes emerging regenerative approaches. It does not provide a demonstrated human result showing restoration of sustained physeal growth. It also does not identify the specific fat or cement interposition materials named in the earlier research, provide a numerical treatment success rate, or substantiate the detailed proliferative and hypertrophic architecture claim.

The earlier research reports that an MSC systematic review identified by PMC12553497 contained animal studies and no included human studies, and attributes low success and frequent bar recurrence after resection and fillers to a Zhang and colleagues review in Advanced Healthcare Materials, first published 3 October 2025, DOI 10.1002/adhm.202501906. These remain unverified reports within the supplied research. The MSC account was described as snippet-level access with no extracted author byline, and the Zhang account as abstract-level access with an incomplete byline. Neither underlying text nor a saved artifact for either review was available to the supplied evidence review. Their study selection, findings, and exact scope therefore cannot establish the absence of human regeneration; this evidence limitation does not show that the reported findings are false.

USC Stem Cell’s article by Katharine Gammon, dated 28 October 2026, describes Zhaoyang Liu’s basic research on the cells and signals that sustain growth plates. The supplied review had complete article text and confirms its statement that there is no established way to reopen a closed growth plate. This is relevant developmental context, but closed-plate reopening is a separate problem from repairing an injured plate that remains open. The article does not establish the status of every approach to injured open-plate regeneration.

Across the supplied evidence, the biological repair goal and ongoing research are documented, but achievement of sustained functional regeneration in an injured human physis is not demonstrated. The supplied search record is empty, so these materials cannot establish comprehensive field status as of 1 November 2026. The appropriate conclusion is limited to what this evidence establishes, rather than a universal claim that no successful human result exists.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: enroll children with more than two years of growth remaining and a bony bar occupying at least one quarter of a distal femoral or proximal tibial physis. Show restoration of functional physeal cartilage, resumed longitudinal growth attributable to the repaired region, and prevention of recurrent bridging throughout remaining growth. These eligibility choices define a proposed test population; they are not established clinical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Restored physeal cartilage sustains growth without bridging throughout remaining growth

completion_criteria.text: Proposed final outcomes would include a limb-length discrepancy within 5 mm and corresponding angular alignment within 5 degrees of an unaffected opposite limb at skeletal maturity, without an external fixation frame. These tolerances and the frame-free requirement are proposed targets, not validated thresholds or demonstrated feasibility. Baseline discrepancy and alignment, remaining growth, and any accompanying corrective procedures should be recorded so that resumed growth can be distinguished from correction of existing deformity.
completion_criteria.label: Frame-free maturity: limb-length discrepancy within 5 mm, angular alignment within 5°

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence should connect tissue restoration with function: serial assessment of length and alignment, imaging of the repaired region and possible recurrent bars, and appropriate evidence of physeal tissue organization. Animal histology alone would not qualify without demonstrated continued longitudinal growth. Likewise, a favorable final limb measurement would not by itself prove regeneration if other interventions could explain it.
completion_criteria.label: Evidence connects restored physeal tissue organization with continued longitudinal growth

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements would include consistent results across multiple patients, independent clinical replication, transparent reporting of failures and additional procedures, and follow-up through skeletal maturity. Evaluation should address disproportionate growth, recurrent arrest, unintended bone formation, and other treatment-related harms. The unaffected opposite limb is a useful comparator only when it is an appropriate reference for that patient.
completion_criteria.label: Independent clinical replication through skeletal maturity with transparent outcome reporting

completion_criteria.text: Demonstrations should state their practical boundaries, including anatomical site, bar size and location, injury cause, pre-existing deformity, remaining growth, and treatment requirements. Success in the proposed knee-region population would establish demonstrated breadth within that population; it would not prove effectiveness in every physis, after every injury, or after normal growth-plate closure.
completion_criteria.label: Report demonstrated anatomical and clinical boundaries of treatment effectiveness

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ORT-01, Adult epimorphic regeneration of a functional limb, shares the challenge of rebuilding organized living tissue, but requires coordinated restoration of an entire limb. ORT-09 is a narrower developmental repair capability in a growing skeleton; success would not establish adult limb regeneration.

Roster-based synthesis: ORT-02, Biological restoration of the osteoarthritic synovial joint, and ORT-05, Restoration of the intervertebral disc as a living load-bearing organ, overlap with ORT-09 in cartilage biology and tissue engineering. Their functional targets differ: a growth plate must generate longitudinal bone growth and eventually mature, while joint and disc restoration address their respective organ functions. Cartilage formation alone cannot serve as a common completion criterion.

Roster-based synthesis: ORT-08, Anatomically precise and reversible control of osteogenesis, is closely related because growth-plate repair must permit bone formation in the proper developmental sequence while preventing a pathological bridge. Spatial control of osteogenesis could be an enabling capability, but controlling bone formation alone would not demonstrate restoration of physeal cartilage or coordinated longitudinal growth.

Roster-based synthesis: ORT-10, Single-episode restoration of segmental long bone by vascularized, remodelable bone, concerns replacing missing bone. ORT-09 concerns restoring the structure that generates additional bone length during growth. Both require integration with a long bone, but successful segmental bone repair does not establish growth-plate regeneration, and restored physeal function does not establish repair of a segmental bone defect.

Roster-based synthesis: ORT-04, Regeneration of the load-bearing tendon–bone enthesis; ORT-06, Force-bearing skeletal muscle after volumetric muscle loss; and ORT-07, Meaningful motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps, share the requirement that regenerated tissue demonstrate sustained function rather than favorable appearance alone. Their respective interface, force-generation, and nerve-recovery outcomes remain distinct from longitudinal growth.

Roster-based synthesis: ORT-03, Eradication of mature biofilm in bone and on orthopedic implants without removing the reconstruction, addresses infection control. It could be relevant where infection complicates a reconstruction, but eliminating infection would not itself restore a damaged physis. Conversely, ORT-09 does not establish biofilm eradication or infection-specific regenerative efficacy.

change_log.change: Preserved ORT-09 and its title while defining the target as functional repair of an injured, still-open physis.
change_log.reason: The review supports this identity and distinguishes it from reopening a mature plate or other skeletal growth interventions.

change_log.change: Replaced permanent-cartilage language with sustained growth, prevention of pathological bridging, normal turnover, and eventual maturation.
change_log.reason: Normal growth includes cartilage replacement by bone; suppressing all ossification would misstate the biological objective.

change_log.change: Separated prevention of further deformity from reversal of deformity already present.
change_log.reason: Restored growth does not automatically correct accumulated shortening or angulation.

change_log.change: Retained fewer corrective procedures as a conditional benefit and qualified treatment comparisons and infection-specific implications.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence supports the injury mechanism but does not demonstrate these clinical outcomes or comparisons.

change_log.change: Preserved tissue-zone organization as an intended architectural feature while identifying its limited evidentiary support.
change_log.reason: The earlier research contains useful explanatory detail, but the supplied abstract does not substantiate the specific proliferative and hypertrophic organization.

change_log.change: Used the supported description of bridge resection and interpositional grafting without asserting specific materials or numerical success rates.
change_log.reason: The abstract supports the treatment limitation but not the earlier fat, cement, or quantitative efficacy implications.

change_log.change: Preserved the MSC and Zhang review reports with their access, attribution, and verification limitations.
change_log.reason: Their underlying evidence was unavailable to the supplied review; omitting them entirely would lose research context, while presenting them as verified would overstate support.

change_log.change: Separated USC’s closed-plate reopening statement from the status of injured open-plate repair and limited the November 2026 status conclusion.
change_log.reason: The USC article addresses a distinct problem, and the empty search record cannot support comprehensive absence claims.

change_log.change: Preserved all proposed numerical completion targets and clarified comparison, follow-up, attribution, reproducibility, and applicability.
change_log.reason: The targets are coherent proposals but are not established standards; convincing regeneration requires sustained function and interpretable outcomes.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry without merging their identities.
change_log.reason: Shared regenerative methods and enabling capabilities do not make their functional endpoints interchangeable.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not determine whether sustained functional regeneration of an injured human physis has been demonstrated elsewhere; the search record provides no comprehensive coverage.
The identity, inclusion criteria, date coverage, and findings of the MSC review identified as PMC12553497 remain unverified beyond the research’s snippet-level report.
The Zhang review’s complete attribution, treatment comparisons, and recurrence findings remain unverified because its underlying text was unavailable.
The specific tissue-zone architecture and named interposition materials require evidence beyond the supplied Rasouli–Wenke abstract.
The proposed remaining-growth requirement, bar-size threshold, 5 mm and 5 degree tolerances, and frame-free condition require clinical justification and feasibility assessment.
Whether restored growth could correct existing deformity, reduce later procedures, or succeed after different injury causes remains to be demonstrated.

The review’s recommendation to omit the unavailable MSC and Zhang findings from the main status account was not adopted literally: they were retained as explicitly unverified research reports to preserve useful context without treating them as established evidence.

brief.title: Restoring a child’s bone growth after injury
possible: A child whose injured leg has stopped growing properly could regain growth in the damaged region. Repair would restore the growth plate, the cartilage that lengthens a growing bone, and keep a harmful bridge of bone from forming across it again.
why: Restoring coordinated growth could prevent a child’s legs from becoming increasingly unequal or misaligned. It could also reduce accumulated deformity and the need for later corrective operations.

sources.who: Mehdi Rasouli and Joseph C Wenke
sources.showed: Their review describes how bone bridges interrupt childhood bone growth, why surgical removal often fails to restore growth-plate function, and approaches being explored for biological repair.
sources.quote: Conventional treatments focus on surgical resection of the bone bridge and interpositional grafting, but these approaches often fail to restore the native architecture or biological function of the physis, and recurrence is common.
sources.cited_for: Existing surgery often leaves growth-plate function impaired, motivating efforts to regenerate the tissue.
sources.not_established: Durable restoration of growth in an injured human growth plate remains to be demonstrated.

sources.who: Zhaoyang Liu and her team at the University of Southern California
sources.showed: The team is studying cells that sustain growth-plate cartilage. Several candidate cell-surface sensors appear especially abundant in cells that can produce new cartilage cells.
sources.quote: Several candidate receptors appear to be highly enriched in the stem and progenitor-like cells.
sources.cited_for: Basic research is identifying cells and signals involved in maintaining growth plates.
sources.not_established: Whether targeting these cells and signals can restore sustained growth after injury remains an open question.

shown: Rasouli and Wenke describe repair strategies involving cells, materials that support new tissue, and biological signals. Liu’s USC team is investigating how growth-plate cartilage maintains itself. These efforts identify possible routes toward restoring growth.
missing: A repair must restore sustained bone lengthening in children while preventing a recurrent bone bridge.
The repaired region must grow in coordination with the surviving plate and mature normally.
Follow-up must establish lasting benefits and harms through the end of childhood growth.

milestones.label: Repaired cartilage keeps growing through childhood
milestones.explanation: Children with substantial growth remaining and a large bone bridge near the knee would have to regain growth from the repaired region without recurrent bridging. This would establish lasting growth-plate function.

milestones.label: Leg length and alignment meet targets at maturity
milestones.explanation: At maturity, leg length and alignment would have to meet the proposed tolerances without an external fixation frame. Accounting for starting deformity and other procedures would clarify the repair’s contribution.

milestones.label: Restored tissue demonstrably produces continued bone growth
milestones.explanation: Repeated measurements and imaging would have to connect organized growth-plate tissue with continued bone lengthening. This would establish that the repaired tissue produces growth.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce lasting clinical results
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce results across patients through maturity, reporting failures, harms and additional procedures. This would establish reproducibility and reveal treatment risks.

milestones.label: Treatment effectiveness has clearly demonstrated boundaries
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to report which bone sites, injury causes, bridge sizes and patient circumstances respond, alongside treatment requirements. This would establish where the repair works.

uncertain: The proposed eligibility rules, final measurement tolerances and requirement to avoid an external frame need clinical justification.
Whether restored growth can correct existing shortening or angulation remains open.
Effectiveness across different injury causes and growth-plate locations remains to be established.

page.title: Regeneration of an injured growth plate
page.definition: Repair of an injured, still-open physis—the cartilage that lengthens a growing bone—restores cartilage that sustains longitudinal growth. The repaired region grows without recurrent pathological bony bridging and undergoes normal skeletal maturation.

goal.need: Growth-plate injuries account for up to 30% of paediatric fractures, according to a 2026 review. A bony bridge across the injured cartilage can interrupt lengthening and produce limb-length discrepancy or angular deformity. Surgical bridge removal and interposition often fail to restore the plate’s architecture or biological function, and recurrence is common.

statements.body: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, NIH, funded project R01AR082426
statements.quote: the need for novel therapeutic strategies to prevent bone formation at the injury site and to allow epiphyseal cartilage to resume growth.
statements.context: The project, Growth plate cartilage stem cells for skeletal repair after injury, began on 15 December 2023. The passage is from its funded project summary.

statements.quote: Rarely, a bony bridge will form across the fracture line, stunting the growth of the bone or causing the bone to curve.
statements.context: The patient guidance was reviewed by members of the Pediatric Orthopaedic Society of North America.

completion.title: Repaired human growth plates sustain growth without recurrent bony bridging through skeletal maturity.
completion.criterion: In children with an injured, still-open physis, repaired cartilage at the injured region generates longitudinal growth through skeletal maturity, without recurrent pathological bony bridging or progressive angulation attributable to renewed arrest. Serial imaging and growth measurements establish the repaired region’s contribution to lengthening, accounting for concomitant corrective procedures. This is an Atlas fallback without numerical growth-rate, length-discrepancy or angular tolerances.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external definition of successful human growth-plate regeneration was located.
completion.basis: Searches of AAOS/POSNA guidance, NIH project targets, FDA cellular-therapy guidance and clinical-trial records found no physis-specific completion threshold. The fallback combines the NIH objective of resumed growth with AAOS follow-up to skeletal maturity for femoral, tibial and complicated injuries. AAOS recommends that follow-up duration for injury surveillance; it does not define regeneration success.

milestones.title: Animal physeal repair forms cartilage and reduces growth disturbance versus controls at P < 0.05.
milestones.criterion: Repair produces cartilage at an injured animal physis, prevents pathological bridging and reduces growth disturbance. Gültekin and colleagues assessed tibial length discrepancy, angulation and histology at week 12, using P < 0.05. Their rabbit study used 18 recipients, six per group, plus three donors. Median tibial length discrepancies were 2.5 mm with chondrocytes, 8.5 mm with mesenchymal stem cells and 12.0 mm in controls; between-group differences in discrepancy and angulation were significant. Histology showed cartilage and prevention of bridging in treated defects.
milestones.set_by: Gültekin and colleagues, published rabbit experimental protocol, 2020; a study-specific test for proximal tibial injury, without an established human equivalent.
milestones.threshold_quote: Statistical significance was determined at P < 0.05.

milestones.title: A regenerative growth-plate treatment is administered to a child in a clinical study.
milestones.criterion: Clinical administration reaches the first-human-use stage recognised in FDA’s general cellular-therapy development framework. CSCR/CMC Vellore’s 2019–2020 report records three treated cases in a planned 15-child phase I safety study of autologous iliac-crest physeal chondrocytes for physeal bars. It also describes pilot follow-up at five years without defining success or supplying quantitative efficacy results. The institutional report is not peer reviewed and does not establish completed safety or efficacy endpoints.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Considerations for the Design of Early-Phase Clinical Trials of Cellular and Gene Therapy Products, section I; a general development stage. The Indian study is an example of human use, without implied FDA authorisation.
milestones.threshold_quote:
the initial introduction of an investigational
new drug into humans

milestones.title: A controlled human study establishes restored growth attributable to repair of the injured physis.
milestones.criterion: A controlled clinical study in children meets a prespecified functional growth endpoint and establishes that regenerative treatment restores longitudinal growth from the repaired region. The comparison accounts for physeal-bar excision and accompanying corrective procedures; imaging assesses recurrent bridging and measurements assess length and alignment over the protocol’s follow-up. The endpoint, follow-up duration and statistical decision rule must come from that protocol. No qualifying controlled result or physis-specific numerical success threshold was located.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback after searches for controlled physeal-regeneration trials and registered endpoints. FDA’s adequate-and-well-controlled-study standard supports the comparison principle but supplies no growth-plate endpoint.

not_found: No regulator, professional society, roadmap or prize definition of successful human growth-plate regeneration was located.
The WHO/CTRI record for CTRI/2012/05/002638 could not be opened, so its registered endpoints and follow-up could not be verified.
No controlled human efficacy result or clinical results paper establishing regeneration through skeletal maturity was located.
